title: TESS eclipse times of HD 303514 move by up to 100 minutes within one year; a near-coplanar third star on a 593-day orbit fits these times and the eclipse fading, and the eclipses stop near 2030
abstract: HD 303514 is a 19.9-day eclipsing binary whose eclipses faded from about 17 percent depth in 2002 to 0.7 percent in 2026. A prior study inferred a third star but did not measure eclipse times. We timed 15 TESS eclipses (QLP light curves, 2019-2026) and 19 eclipses in our own cutout photometry. Relative to a linear ephemeris, the times move between -51 and +53 minutes (chi-square 287 for 12 degrees of freedom); the secondary eclipses moved by 94 minutes in 0.8 years. A light-travel-time orbit fits the times only with a mass function of 110 solar masses or more, so the shifts are mostly dynamical. Newtonian three-body fits to the times and to 15 published depths find one solution family: outer period 593 (582-603) days, outer eccentricity 0.24, mutual inclination 3.4 (2.8-4.0) degrees, and mass ratio m3/(m1+m2) = 0.85 (0.69-1.01), independent of the assumed pair mass. The best fit has chi-square 11.4 for 31 terms; no other outer-period range comes within 45. The same model makes the inner orbit precess with a period of about 116 years, which explains the fading, and it is stable for 100,000 years. Not fitted, the 2001-2009 ASAS-3 eclipse times agree with the back-extrapolated best model for five of six values; the 2002 primary value differs by 4.4 sigma. The model predicts the last eclipse deeper than 0.1 percent in 2029.8 (68 percent range 2029.6-2030.5) and a radial-velocity range of the eclipsing pair of about 54 km/s in 2027-2029. Limits: assumed twin point masses and pair mass, constant dilutions, incomplete global search, a short MCMC, inherited depth data, and no spectra.
